1 Introduction
Road transport is a leading source of greenhouse gases and local air pollutants. The
associated health, economic, and societal consequences are substantial and well docu-
mented (OECD 2014; World Health Organization 2025). An increasingly popular policy
tool to handle these external costs is the creation of Low Emission Zones (LEZs): urban
areas that restrict access to vehicles that fail to meet certain environmental standards.
Introduced in 2008 in several German cities, LEZs are now found all over Europe and in
many cities around the world, including Shanghai, Beijing, Haifa, Seoul, and Jakarta.1
Even some U.S. cities have begun experimenting with more targeted versions of LEZs,
particularly for freight and last-mile delivery.
An often overlooked aspect of LEZs is the significant variation in their design, par-
ticularly concerning the geographic scope of the covered area and the types of restricted
vehicles. For example, the LEZ in Berlin, implemented in 2008, spans 88 km2, restricts
some, but not all, gasoline and diesel cars, and imposes different geographic restrictions
among its restricted cars. In contrast, the LEZ in Madrid, known as Madrid Central and
implemented a decade later, covers a much smaller area, of just 5 km2, but restricts all
gasoline and diesel cars, making no geographic distinction among them.
Such wide variation raises important policy-design questions, which motivate this
paper: What is the optimal LEZ size, and should some cars be restricted more, or later,
than others? A central goal of a LEZ is to achieve sustained reductions in air pollution
by creating incentives for drivers to switch to cleaner modes of transportation, whether
cleaner cars or public transit (Ayuntamiento de Madrid 2018, arts. 22–23, p. 139).2 Given
this goal, we show that the answers to the above questions follow a bang-bang logic: for
a welfare-maximizing planner, a LEZ should be either as large as politically feasible or
not implemented at all. Moreover, when less-polluting vehicles such as hybrids are to be
restricted, such a planner restricts them in the same way as other restricted cars, but
later.
Using Madrid’s LEZ as both motivation and evidence, we initiate our analysis by
assessing its impact on the adoption of hybrids and electric vehicles (EVs), which, along
with liquefied petroleum gas or compressed natural gas vehicles (LPG/CNG), are exempt
from the restriction. Looking at sales of new cars and comparing Madrid to other cities in
Spain, we estimate a synthetic difference-in-differences model (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021)
and show that Madrid’s LEZ was effective in accelerating the adoption of hybrids and
1By 2024, 363 LEZs were active in 15 European countries, including 175 in Italy, 77 in Germany, and 36
in Spain (Delgado-Lindeman et al. 2025).
2This goal is consistent with EU policy, under which LEZs are an important instrument for cities seeking to
comply with EU air-quality standards (Ayuntamiento de Madrid 2018, p. 134). It is also consistent with
the findings of Bernardo, Fageda, and Flores-Fillol (2021), who, using data from several European LEZs
over the period 2008–2016, find that LEZs reduced pollution but not congestion, which they attribute
to extensive-margin adjustments toward cleaner cars rather than intensive-margin adjustments, i.e.,
reductions in vehicle use.
2
LPG/CNG vehicles, and to a lesser extent EVs, while also reducing the sales of new
gasoline and diesel cars.
These findings raise policy questions that reach beyond Madrid’s LEZ design. Was it
welfare-improving to fully exempt LPG/CNG and hybrid cars? Two alternatives arise. A
spatial alternative would restrict these cars less stringently than gasoline and diesel cars—
barring them from a smaller zone, as in Berlin’s tiered design. A temporal alternative
would treat them as transition technologies: unrestricted for now, but with an announced
timetable under which they later face the same restrictions as gasoline and diesel cars.
Both alternatives would make EVs more attractive relative to them, but through different
channels, and at different costs to their current owners and to drivers thinking of switching
away from gasoline. So the natural question is: How do the two alternatives compare,
and when does either yield higher welfare than Madrid’s full exemption of LPG/CNG
and hybrids?
We shed light on these and related questions with a simple dynamic model of three
horizontally differentiated car types (gasoline, hybrids, EVs) that also differ in their emis-
sion rates. Hybrids—which represent any intermediate technology such as LPG/CNG—
pollute less than gasoline cars but more than EVs. The model formalizes the bang-bang
rationale: to maximize welfare, all restricted vehicles should be treated equally, and
the LEZ should be either as large as possible or not implemented at all if it falls be-
low a minimum scale. Within this rationale, hybrids may still qualify as a transition
technology—kept as unrestricted as EVs for some time, and then as restricted as gaso-
line cars. This transition-technology design, however, may require commitment from the
planner.
Unlike price-based instruments, such as taxes and tradable quotas, which operate
under an efficient rationing rule, LEZs operate under an inefficient (e.g., proportional)
rationing rule, leading to quasi-convex welfare functions.3 To see this, imagine a social
planner who introduces a small pollution tax on dirty vehicles. The welfare impact of this
tax is confined to the marginal drivers who switch to cleaner cars in response to the tax.
Importantly, social welfare is unaffected by the tax impact on inframarginal drivers—
those who do not switch. Initially, the welfare loss to switchers from moving away from
their preferred (i.e., no-intervention) car is smaller than the social welfare gain from
reduced emissions. The planner finds it optimal to increase the tax up to its Pigouvian
level, where the (concave) welfare function reaches its maximum level. Importantly, unless
set far above its Pigouvian level, a tax always increases social welfare, no matter how
small.4
Because LEZs involve inefficient rationing, they differ fundamentally from price-
based instruments; under some conditions, even the best LEZ may yield lower welfare
3See Tirole (1988) for more on rationing rules.
4Shadow costs of public funds may affect the optimal tax in either direction according to a Ramsey
formula but never eliminate it (Laffont and Tirole 1996).
3
than having no LEZ. To see this, consider a small LEZ that restricts only gasoline cars.
Unlike a tax, a LEZ imposes a welfare cost on every inframarginal driver who continues
driving gasoline cars. These individuals will have to change their transport mode (e.g.,
to public transit), reroute around the LEZ, or cancel trips altogether. If the number of
inframarginal individuals is large, the welfare losses borne by them can be large relative to
the net welfare gains from the few marginal individuals who switch from gasoline cars to
hybrids or EVs. As a result, a small LEZ may reduce welfare—unless it can be expanded
above a minimum scale, large enough to leave few inframarginal drivers restricted.
This minimum scale is the LEZ size that achieves the same welfare as the no-
intervention outcome. We show that when pollution harm is not too large, or substitution
toward cleaner cars is weak, the minimum scale may not exist, so implementing any LEZ
reduces welfare. In contrast, when pollution harm is relatively large, and substitution is
strong, the minimum scale can be small, even zero, meaning that almost any LEZ would
increase welfare in our model. Even then, the quasi-convexity of the welfare function
implies that welfare is highest at the largest possible LEZ.
This bang-bang logic—to reduce the number of inframarginal consumers of restricted
cars as much as possible—also explains why, in our model, all restricted cars should be
treated equally, i.e., subject to the largest politically feasible LEZ. We also show that, in
many cases, the planner maximizes welfare by treating hybrids as a transition technology:
initially exempt from the restrictions, but subject to them at a later stage. Anticipating
the declining value of hybrids, and provided the planner can commit to the announced
future restrictions, some individuals may choose to switch away from hybrids before
the restrictions take effect.5 Consequently, fewer hybrids remain in circulation by the
time the restriction arrives, reducing the cost of imposing it. In this sense, a LEZ with
a transition technology works more like a price-based instrument: it affects consumer
choices at the margin without destroying value for inframarginal consumers before the
restriction becomes active.6
We conduct an empirical evaluation of Madrid’s LEZ, focusing on new-car adoption
and welfare. Because car prices and preferences cannot be projected far ahead, we esti-
mate impacts around policy implementation and ask whether, at that time, the necessary
conditions for even considering a LEZ were met. That is, we ask whether there was a
minimum scale above which some LEZ design could improve welfare. We focus on house-
holds buying a new car, since that is where fleet composition changes: a second-hand
purchase mostly reallocates the existing stock. Our welfare estimates account for the
private costs of switching away from households’ preferred options, the utility loss borne
5Some switch to electric vehicles, while others move to gasoline cars; the latter case is less relevant, as
gasoline cars are already restricted.
6Our definition of a transition technology differs from alternative notions, which are often based on the
idea that electric vehicles remain too expensive or unfamiliar to serve as a viable outside option for many
gasoline drivers. Under that view, hybrids should remain unrestricted until these concerns dissipate.
While our definition is not in conflict with that view, it is fundamentally different.
4
by those who continue to buy restricted cars, and the lifetime externalities of the chosen
vehicles.
In the spirit of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995), we estimate demand for new cars
using registration data covering new cars sold in Spain from 2015 to 2019, together with
their prices and characteristics. Consumers’ preferences for cars, and their willingness to
pay to avoid the LEZ, vary with income and other consumer characteristics. Consistent
with our motivating evidence, we find that some consumers switch from gasoline and
diesel cars toward hybrids, LPG/CNG cars, and EVs. But the resulting externality
savings fall well short of the private losses: consumer surplus falls substantially more than
the reduction in externality costs. The private cost of tightening the restriction exceeds
the emission benefit throughout the range of intensities we evaluate, so a larger LEZ
would not have helped; nor would extending the restrictions to LPG/CNG vehicles and
hybrids, which raises the share of gasoline and diesel cars without materially increasing
EV adoption.
These negative results could be reversed under a LEZ design that also restricts
LPG/CNG and hybrids, if the following conditions are met: a substantially higher social
cost of emissions combined with a larger restricted zone, or stronger substitution toward
EVs. All this suggests that, at least in Madrid, the necessary conditions for considering a
LEZ in the first place were not satisfied. It also points to a broader conclusion: for a LEZ
to improve welfare, there must be fewer drivers buying gasoline and diesel cars, and the
barriers to adopting cleaner ones must be lower. For EVs, these barriers include limited
access to charging, short perceived driving range, and long charging times (Rosales-
Tristancho et al. 2022).
It is important to point out that these negative results abstract from any local
benefits that a LEZ may bring to residents and businesses within the restricted area,
such as safer streets and improved public space. This raises the broader question of
who ultimately determines LEZ design. This paper takes the stance of a planner who
cares about overall welfare. A narrower perspective is that of a decision maker who cares
mostly about the welfare of residents in the restricted area. A local constituency may
evaluate a small LEZ quite differently, and possibly quite favorably, than such a planner.
The wide variation in LEZ size that we observe—with Berlin and Madrid providing good
examples—may partly reflect these different perspectives. Our contribution should be
understood from the broader perspective: how best to use the LEZ instrument when the
objective is overall welfare.7
Our paper contributes to four strands of the literature. First, we contribute to
the vast literature on car markets. Closest to our work are the papers by Adda and
Cooper (2000) and Gillingham et al. (2022), which pay explicit attention to both new
and second-hand units and market dynamics. However, we depart from both papers in
7And in doing so, we completely abstract from the political-economy question of why cities opt for LEZs
as opposed to more efficient instruments.
5
important ways. Adda and Cooper (2000) consider a single type of car, abstracting from
any horizontal differentiation—both in preferences and pollution rates—which lies at the
core of our framework. Gillingham et al. (2022), by contrast, offer a rich framework with
various degrees of differentiation (in preferences and pollution) but, by focusing on sta-
tionary equilibria, abstract from aggregate shocks that may evolve over time and generate
transition dynamics. Unlike both papers, we study how a market with differentiated cars
adjusts over time to a LEZ. This adjustment matters for policy design, especially when
hybrids can be treated as a transition technology.8
Second, we contribute to the growing literature evaluating the performance of LEZ
programs around the world.9 Several papers document the positive health impacts of
LEZs, driven by reductions in local air pollution (e.g., Klauber et al. 2024; Beshir and
Fichera 2022; Margaryan 2021; Gehrsitz 2017), although these benefits come at the cost
of restricted mobility (Sarmiento, W¨agner, and Zaklan 2023). Others provide reduced-
form evidence on the effects of LEZs on traffic, finding reductions in congestion within the
restricted area (Galdon-Sanchez et al. 2023) that are often temporary, negative spillovers
to adjacent areas (Tassinari 2024), or simply no effects (Bernardo, Fageda, and Flores-
Fillol 2021; Garson et al. 2026).
Only a few papers study the effects of LEZs on the adoption of lower-emission
vehicles, which are central to the policy-design questions at the core of our analysis. An
early exception is Wolff (2014), who shows that German LEZs induced residents living
close to restricted areas to increase their adoption of low-emission vehicles. More recently,
also in the context of German LEZs, Aydin, Gehrsitz, and Traxler (2024) find that highly
polluting vehicles were replaced by cleaner gasoline cars.10 These empirical findings are
consistent with the theoretical model we develop in this paper, as well as with the evidence
on Madrid’s LEZ that motivates it. However, none of these papers evaluate whether the
effects of induced low-emission vehicle adoption are large enough to offset the welfare
costs associated with restricted mobility and distorted choices.
Third, we contribute to the extensive literature comparing the performance of dif-
ferent policy instruments, typically categorized as either price-based (e.g., taxes, tradable
quotas) or command-and-control (e.g., emissions and technology standards). While LEZs
clearly fall within the command-and-control (CAC) category, they differ from other in-
struments in this group due to the bang-bang rationale underlying their optimal design.
Under most standard CAC instruments, the “marginal-inframarginal” tradeoff at the
8Our theory also connects to the work of Gavazza, Lizzeri, and Roketskiy (2014) on trade frictions in the
second-hand market. We abstract from vertical differentiation, which is essential to generate trade in
their model; nevertheless, second-hand-market trade may still emerge in our setting with the introduction
of a LEZ or a tax.
9LEZs impose differential restrictions across vehicles, unlike some early programs that applied uniformly to
all cars and proved counterproductive (e.g., Davis 2008; Gallego, Montero, and Salas 2013). Differential
treatment also features in the vintage-specific restrictions studied by Barahona, Gallego, and Montero
(2020).
10Other papers have analyzed the impacts of alternative instruments on fleet composition, including con-
gestion pricing (e.g., Isaksen and Johansen 2021; B¨orjesson et al. 2012).
6
core of a LEZ design does not arise. As a result, the welfare function remains concave,
and the bang-bang rationale does not apply (see, e.g., Baumol and Oates 1988; Ellerman
et al. 2000).11
Relatedly, Almagro et al. (2024), Durrmeyer and Mart´ınez (2026), Ater et al. (2026),
and Cook and Li (2025) quantify the welfare effects of different urban-transportation
policies—road pricing, transit fares, and service frequencies in Chicago; tolls and license-
plate bans in Paris; usage-based congestion pricing in Tel Aviv; and dynamically priced
highway lanes in Seattle, respectively. All four papers hold the private vehicle fleet fixed
and focus on short-run margins. Cook et al. (2025) find that, over its first 18 months, New
York City’s congestion pricing raised traffic speeds but had little effect on air quality. By
contrast, we study a policy instrument whose central welfare tradeoff operates through a
long-run margin: the adoption of lower-emission vehicles.
Finally, we contribute to the literature on time inconsistency in environmental pol-
icy, although through a distinctive channel: in our setting, the commitment problem
does not arise under taxes—it arises only under a LEZ design that involves transition
technologies. This stands in contrast with the standard framing (e.g., Laffont and Tirole

taxes or standards—once agents have invested in irreversible abatement technologies or
R&D. Ours does not follow this expropriation logic but, rather, a pure discounting one:
when hybrids are not so dirty, the initial announcement of their future restriction fails to
induce enough switching toward cleaner options to reduce the number of inframarginal
hybrid users sufficiently to justify restricting them ex post.12

impact on green vehicle adoption. Section 3 develops a dynamic model of car choice and
examines the implications for the optimal LEZ design. Section 4 presents the structural
estimation, and Section 5 conducts the counterfactual analysis. Section 6 concludes.
Additional results and proofs are relegated to the Appendix.

6 Conclusions
We have shown, both theoretically and empirically, that LEZs differ fundamentally
from price-based instruments (e.g., taxes, tradable quotas). A tax on polluting cars, no
matter how small, always increases social welfare by inducing drivers to switch toward
cleaner vehicles, unless, of course, it is set too far above its Pigouvian level. A LEZ that
restricts polluting cars, by contrast, may not be worth considering in the first place. It
must be stringent enough to induce substantial switching while leaving sufficiently few
inframarginal users affected by the restriction; otherwise, having no LEZ may yield higher
welfare. Our estimates suggest that this was the case for Madrid’s LEZ. Although the
policy shifted some buyers toward cleaner cars, the surplus losses it generated far exceeded
the gains from the emissions it saved. Our counterfactual analysis clarifies what it would
take for a LEZ in Madrid to be welfare-improving: LPG/CNG and hybrids would also
have to be restricted, externality damages would have to be much larger, or the residual
demand for polluting vehicles sufficiently flat to generate stronger substitution toward
cleaner alternatives.
These findings also speak to the role of combining LEZs with other instruments.
In Weitzman’s (1974) prices-versus-quantities framework, for example, combining instru-
ments may be optimal because the planner faces a friction: policy cannot be continuously
adjusted as new information arrives. That friction is absent from our framework. If price-
based instruments are available, there is no intrinsic reason to combine them with an
inefficient rationing instrument such as a LEZ, unless they cannot be set at their optimal
levels. In such a case, prices can play a supporting role by reducing the number of infra-
marginal users. By making polluting vehicles less attractive, or cleaner vehicles easier to
adopt, they may help satisfy the necessary conditions under which a LEZ becomes worth
considering.
While our focus in this paper has been strictly on a LEZ’s ability to induce drivers
to switch toward cleaner vehicles, it is important to recognize that such policies may also
generate local benefits for residents and businesses within the restricted area, including
improvements in urban amenities. To the extent that these benefits are quantitatively im-
portant, the relatively limited geographic scope of Madrid’s LEZ may have represented an
adequate way to strike a balance between local welfare gains and city-wide welfare losses
associated with restricting vehicle access. Quantifying this broader tradeoff, however, is
beyond the scope of this paper.

With its 13 November 2026 judgement in the North Sea Fields Case, the Norwegian Supreme Court invalidated the approvals for production from three Norwegian oilfields. In their thoughtful post, Colombo, Gloppen and Robiou du Pont summarise the factual context, case history and key findings. Here I will critically analyse the Court’s findings on the requirements for the environmental impact assessment (EIA) of fossil fuel extraction projects. I argue that, judged in light of the EU EIA Directive’s purpose of advancing transparent and democratically accountable environmental decision-making (preamble, recital 16), the judgement contains both advances and setbacks.
Combustion Emissions
The Directive requires that the EIA process “identify, describe and assess in an appropriate manner […] the direct and indirect significant effects of a project” on various factors, including “climate” (art. 3(1)(c)).
Starting with the steps forward, the Court provides welcome confirmation that the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the combustion of petroleum, including where exported, are indirect “effects” of the project within the meaning of article 3(1) (paras. 143–150). Here, the Court agreed with the EFTA Court’s Advisory Opinion, which the Borgarting Court of Appeal had requested at an earlier stage in the case. It is also consistent with the interpretation given to the Directive by the UK Supreme Court in Finch v Surrey County Council.
More controversial are the Court’s findings on how combustion emissions must be described and assessed under the EIA Directive.
Market substitution
In this regard, the second step forward is the Court’s conclusion – again, consistent with the EFTA Court’s opinion – that the combustion emissions that must be described and assessed pursuant to article 3(1) are the project’s gross combustion emissions (para. 151).
This finding constitutes a decisive rejection of the argument advanced by the Norwegian state that only the project’s “net” emissions need be assessed. This “market substitution argument” is widely deployed by governments and fossil fuel producers around the world in EIA processes. Where accepted, the argument obscures the climatic impact of the assessed project via opaque economic modelling exercises. The Court’s rejection of it is therefore welcome from a democratic accountability perspective, and joins a growing chorus of jurisprudence sceptical of the evidential, factual, philosophical and/or legal basis of market substitution claims.
Cumulative Emissions
The Directive requires that an EIA report describe the effects of the project on the climate including from “the cumulation of effects with other existing and/or approved projects” (Annex IV, point 5(e); see also Annex IV, point 5 second para.). The Court found that, in the case of a petroleum extraction project, this requires an assessment of the project’s emissions cumulatively with the emissions from other petroleum projects on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (para. 178).
Relative to the state’s submission that it is sufficient to assess the climate effects of a project’s emissions in isolation, the Court’s finding advances democratic accountability, as it goes some way toward mitigating the problem, pervasive in EIA law, of “death by a thousand cuts”.
However, in my estimation the Court did not go far enough. I have argued elsewhere that the most appropriate scope of cumulative effects assessment in the climate context is the cumulative historical (past) and reasonably foreseeable (future) emissions from other project-based sources of emissions globally. This approach, I argue, is appropriate in light of the plain fact that anthropogenic climate change is caused by cumulative global GHG emissions from various kinds of projects. It is also consistent with the Directive’s broad definition of “project” (art. 1(2)(a)), the case law (paras. 45–46) of the European Court of Justice (ECJ), and guidance provided by both the European Commission (p. 50, citing the ECJ case just alluded to) and the UK Government (p. 12).
The Norwegian Supreme Court provides two reasons—one principled, one practical—for limiting the scope of the cumulative effects assessment to Norwegian petroleum projects. The principled reason is that the Norwegian petroleum authorities only have jurisdiction to permit petroleum extraction within Norway (para. 167). But this is a non sequitur. The requirement in question is to assess the effects of a project in light of cumulative emissions. The decision-maker does not need to have jurisdictional authority over any of the other projects that contribute to those cumulative effects to undertake such an assessment.
The Court’s reasoning has counterintuitive implications that undermine the informational and environmental purposes of the Directive. Imagine there exists a fragile ecosystem traversing the border between Norwegian and UK waters, and that the UK had approved oil drilling that, cumulatively, would push the ecosystem just shy of collapse. On the Court’s logic, the Norwegian authorities would have to ignore those cumulative effects when assessing the local biodiversity impacts of an oil extraction project proposed on the Norwegian side of the border, even if the latter project’s impacts would trigger the ecosystem’s collapse. That would be absurd (not to mention a prima facie violation of Norway’s international legal duty to prevent environmental harm).
The Court’s practical reason is that expanding the scope to include projects of other kinds and in other jurisdictions would be excessively burdensome (paras. 167–168). However, as I have pointed out, conservative estimates of global project-based emissions from committed fossil fuel projects (i.e. operating projects plus projects that have been approved or received a final investment decision) are readily available at zero cost. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), in its Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), synthesised scientific evidence of cumulative emissions from existing and planned fossil fuel-consuming infrastructure globally, and research since the AR6 has established the equivalent estimates for emissions embodied in fossil fuel-extraction projects. These could be used as conservative proxies (i.e. industry-favourable underestimates) of cumulative emissions from other projects.
The Court’s burdensomeness finding is even more puzzling when read in light of its claim, a few paragraphs later, that the requirement to assess cumulative emissions from all Norwegian projects would not be unduly burdensome (para. 176). Given that no such cumulative emissions estimates currently exist for Norwegian-only projects, carrying out such an assessment would in fact be more burdensome than the global approach I propose.
The Court (para. 177) also noted the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) conclusion in its climate change Advisory Opinion (paras. 272–273, 276) that states must assess cumulative effects as part of their duty to exercise due diligence to prevent significant harm to the climate system. However, inexplicably, the Supreme Court appears to have assumed that the Opinion (i) is merely persuasive authority from a different jurisdiction, rather than bearing on the interpretation of the EIA Directive; and (ii) supports the Supreme Court’s favoured limitation of the scope of cumulative effects assessment to Norwegian projects, rather than projects globally. Both interpretive assumptions are questionable (space constraints preclude a detailed analysis here, but regarding (i) see Case C-341/95 para. 20; and regarding (ii) see the ICJ Opinion paras. 276–279 and 298).
Global Carbon Budgets
The Borgarting Court of Appeal held that the EIA must assess the project’s emissions in light of a remaining global carbon budget. The Supreme Court disagreed, holding that no such obligation can be derived from the Directive or from Norway’s international legal obligations.
In my view, the most natural basis for inferring such a requirement from the Directive stems from the obligation to assess the (likely) significant effects of a project in an appropriate manner (art. 3(1)), since the assessment of significance necessitates contextualisation of the size of an environmental effect (a scientific matter) with reference to the importance of the relevant environmental receptor (a normative matter) (see, e.g., the EU’s EIA reporting guidance, pp. 47–49). Annex IV, point 5 (second para.) of the Directive indicates where to look for the relevant normative benchmark: the description of the likely significant effects of a project on the factors specified in article 3(1) (including “climate”) “should take into account the environmental protection objectives established at Union or Member State level which are relevant to the project”. The temperature goal of the Paris Agreement (art. 2(1)(a)), as interpreted by the ICJ (para. 224) and endorsed by the Union, is to limit warming to within 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. That goal is the most relevant environmental protection objective for the purpose of assessing the significance of combustion emissions, especially where exported (since national targets/budgets don’t usually count exported emissions). A carbon budget is a scientifically robust, easy-to-understand means of conveying the volume of carbon dioxide that can be emitted while remaining within a specified temperature goal. A remaining global carbon budget for limiting warming to within 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels (with at least a 50% probability – and arguably a higher, more precautionary probability) is, therefore, the most appropriate means of assessing whether the project’s emissions (cumulatively with emissions from other existing and approved projects globally) are consistent with achieving the 1.5°C objective.
However, in the Supreme Court’s view (paras. 181–183), the word “should” in the quoted sentence of Annex IV indicates that taking account of environmental protection objectives is not mandatory; the Court noted the absence of case law from the ECJ finding that “should”, in that sentence, means “shall”. Yet, as the Supreme Court acknowledged earlier (para. 163), the ECJ has found that the preceding sentence in the same paragraph of the Directive, which states that the EIA “should” cover (among other things) cumulative effects, is to be read as “shall”. Surely it would be highly unlikely that the EU authorities intended “should” to have two different meanings when used in precisely the same way in two (indeed, the only two) consecutive sentences of the same paragraph? In any event, even if considered non-binding guidance, the reference to environmental protection objectives in Annex IV is better understood as supplying interpretive guidance for the operationalisation of an appropriate assessment of significance, as indicated above.
The Court also found no basis in international law for the asserted carbon budget requirement. In doing so, the Court perpetuated a myth – often invoked by governments and fossil fuel producers in EIA proceedings – that the Paris Agreement imposes a division of climate mitigation responsibility based on countries’ territorial GHG emissions. Actually, as the Queensland Land Court observed in Waratah Coal (paras. 674–681, 695), the Agreement only envisages a division of emissions accounting/reporting responsibility along territorial lines; mitigation responsibilities do not stop at the border. Similarly, the High Court of Australia in MACH Energy v Denman found legal error in a planning commission’s conflation of the Paris Agreement’s division of responsibility for emissions accounting with the commission’s duty to consider whether to impose conditions on the relevant coal project’s overseas combustion emissions. Alas, the Norwegian Supreme Court, in uncritically repeating the industry-friendly myth that the Paris Agreement divides mitigation responsibilities territorially, has erected a further unjustified obstacle to the use of carbon budgets in EIA, to the great detriment of democratic accountability.
Consequential Effects of Climate Warming
Finally, the Supreme Court rejected the environmental groups’ submission that the EIA process must assess the consequential effects of a project’s climate warming on the other factors listed in article 3(1), such as human health (paras. 192–213). The Court reasoned that this more extensive approach was not justified by the preparatory works to the amendments to the Directive that inserted the references to climate change in Annex IV (paras. 203–210), and that it would be unduly burdensome (paras. 202, 211).
Since no court has, to my knowledge, required such detailed, consequential assessment of a project’s climate effects on other factors, the Court’s ruling on this point can perhaps more aptly be described as a sideways step than a backwards one. Indeed, the Court’s approach is broadly consistent with that taken a month earlier by the High Court of Australia in  Denman when faced with a similar interpretative question concerning New South Wales’ EIA regime.
Nonetheless, the finding is a missed opportunity to improve the transparency and democratic accountability of environmental decision-making – especially in light of the Court’s finding regarding carbon budget analysis. Ultimately, the decision requires merely the assessment of the global temperature increase caused by the project (in cumulation with other domestic petroleum projects). The gravity of that warming impact to most citizens will mean little if conveyed only as an abstract, small-sounding temperature increment. Public participation in EIA processes would be enhanced if proponents were required to assess the impacts of a climate-affecting project on human life and health (among other factors) – consequences the public can much more readily grasp.
Conclusion
Despite some notable advances, the Supreme Court’s judgement falls well short of mandating EIA standards that would significantly advance the public’s understanding of fossil fuel projects’ full climate implications. In particular, the Court’s poorly justified limitation of the scope of cumulative effects assessment and its unwillingness to identify carbon budget analysis as the most appropriate means of assessing the significance of a project’s climate effects mean that the true cumulative impact of new fossil fuel projects on achieving the temperature goal of the Paris Agreement will remain obscured from public view. Consequently, it is likely to remain all too politically convenient for energy ministries in Norway and elsewhere to continue rubber-stamping ever more fossil fuel extraction projects, while global temperatures soar past the 1.5°C goal.

EU countries on Wednesday reached an agreement on an eighth sanctions package against Russia in response to its recent partial military mobilization and illegal annexation of Ukrainian regions.
“(EU) Ambassadors reached a political agreement on new sanctions against Russia, as a strong EU response to Putin's illegal annexation of Ukraine’s territories,” the Czech government, acting as the term president of the Council of the European Union, announced on Twitter.
The measures include a prohibition of transporting oil to non-EU countries above a certain price, mostly affecting the shipping industry of Greece, the Greek Cypriot administration, and Malta.
The bloc also extends its import ban to Russian “steel products, wood pulp, paper, machinery and appliances, chemicals, plastic, cigarettes,” the Czech EU presidency said.
According to European Commission estimates, it would deprive Russia of €7 billion ($6.96 billion) in revenues yearly.
The EU further restricts exports of IT, engineering, and legal services to Russia, as well as expands the list of high-tech goods that cannot be sold to the country.
The new package also adds to the individual sanctions list the people responsible for the mobilization of over 300,000 Russians and the recent organization of referendums in four Ukrainian regions, leading to Moscow last week declaring their “annexation,” a move widely condemned.
Since the beginning of Russia’s war on Ukraine in February, EU sanctions have targeted, among others, President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, banned Russian gold, oil, and coal imports, and exports of luxury and high-tech goods, as well as excluded Russian and Belarusian banks from the international payment system SWIFT.
Ahead of the vote, EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell also reaffirmed the bloc’s support for Ukraine with military aid, diplomatic pressure, and restrictive measures, explaining that despite Putin’s expectations, the “war will not end because Western countries got exhausted.”
He asserted that “Ukraine’s fate is tied to Europe’s.”

25 novembre 2026
Ce 25 novembre, BLOOM avec le FCJE publient une analyse juridique inédite concluant à l’impossibilité pour le législateur de réduire la protection des droits humains, de l’environnement et du climat, à l’occasion de la transposition de la directive européenne sur le devoir de vigilance.
Alors que les travaux sur la transposition ne semblent pas avoir commencé, cette analyse donne un éclairage aux institutions en charge de ce processus.
Cette dernière renforce également l’importance des décisions de justice rendues et à venir sur le fondement de la loi sur le devoir de vigilance.
En 2024, l’Union européenne adoptait une directive historique sur le devoir de vigilance des entreprises (CSDDD). Pilier du Green Deal lancé lors de la première mandature d’Ursula Von der Leyen en tant que présidente de la Commission européenne, ce texte visait à responsabiliser les entreprises au titre des incidences négatives de leur chaîne de valeur sur l’environnement et les droits humains.
Deux ans plus tard, et avant même qu’elle ne puisse être transposée par les États Membres de l’Union dans leur droit national, cette directive a été considérablement affaiblie par le processus « Omnibus I ». Malgré le combat acharné de BLOOM et de nombreuses autres organisations contre ce détricotage du droit européen, l’Omnibus I a été adopté en décembre 2025, porté par une alliance inédite de la droite et de l’extrême droite au Parlement européen.
La directive CSDDD ainsi modifiée par l’Omnibus I doit être transposée en France d’ici juillet 2028.
Entrée en vigueur il y a près de dix ans, la loi française sur le devoir de vigilance1 impose aux grandes entreprises d’identifier, de prévenir et de faire cesser les atteintes graves aux droits humains et à l’environnement résultant de leurs activités, et de celles de leurs filiales et de leurs partenaires commerciaux.
Adoptée en réaction au drame du Rana Plaza, elle a fait de la France le premier pays européen à se doter d’un tel cadre législatif. Elle permet à toute personne ayant un intérêt à agir de saisir le tribunal judiciaire de Paris pour enjoindre à une entreprise de respecter ses obligations, ou pour engager sa responsabilité en cas de manquement.
Les juridictions françaises ont déjà prononcé plusieurs décisions sur le fondement de ce texte, dont une récente relative à la vigilance climatique du groupe TotalÉnergies2.
D’autres actions sont en cours, notamment celle engagée par BLOOM aux côtés de foodwatch contre le géant de l’agro-alimentaire Carrefour pour manquement à ses obligations de vigilance sur sa filière thonière.
Si l’Union européenne s’est inspirée de la France pour élaborer la CSDDD, des divergences existent entre les deux textes posant la question de l’évolution des acquis français dans le cadre de la transposition.
Alors que la France va devoir transposer la CSDDD modifiée par l’Omnibus I, le Forum citoyen pour la justice économique (FCJE) – dont BLOOM est membre – a sollicité Sophie Robin-Olivier, professeure à l’École de droit de l’université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne afin d’analyser ce que cette directive impose au législateur français.
Sa conclusion à l’issue d’une analyse juridique approfondie est sans ambiguïté : la transposition ne peut pas servir de motif pour réduire la protection des droits humains, des droits sociaux, de l’environnement et du climat garantie à ce jour par la loi de 2017 et les décisions rendues sur son fondement.
Partout où le droit français est plus protecteur, il doit être préservé.
Cette consultation que le FCJE rend aujourd’hui publique doit guider les institutions chargées de la transposition.
Le message est clair : la transposition de la CSDDD ne peut pas servir d’excuse pour faire reculer la loi française sur le devoir de vigilance.
20 novembre 2026
La nomination de Jean-Philippe André, ancien président du lobby agroalimentaire ANIA et dirigeant de Haribo jusqu’à fin 2025, à la coprésidence du comité de suivi de la Stratégie nationale pour l’alimentation, la nutrition et le climat (SNANC), constitue une situation manifeste de conflit d’intérêts. Elle remet en question la capacité de l’État à conduire des politiques publiques indépendantes des intérêts industriels et à protéger la santé de la population.
28 septembre 2026
Ce lundi 28 septembre 2026, une coalition de 24 organisations issues de 10 pays européens, coordonnée par BLOOM, a interpellé la Commission européenne pour l’alerter sur l’orientation de la consultation publique organisée cet été pour préparer les futures lignes directrices relatives au devoir de vigilance des entreprises.
Nos organisations dénoncent une approche qui fait de la minimisation des coûts et de la compétitivité l’alpha et l’oméga de cette consultation, au détriment de l’objectif central de la directive : prévenir les atteintes aux droits humains et à l’environnement. Alors que l’administration Trump poursuit ses pressions contre cette législation malgré les affaiblissements déjà entérinés par l’Omnibus I en décembre 2025, la coalition demande à la Commission de préserver l’ambition de la directive, d’associer pleinement les détenteurs de droits à sa mise en œuvre et de publier l’intégralité des contributions reçues dans le cadre de la consultation qui vient de se clore.
19 janvier 2026
En décembre dernier, Intermarché nous faisait miroiter le « mieux manger » avec sa publicité du « loup mal aimé », dans laquelle le loup renonce à manger des animaux au profit de fruits et légumes, sans toutefois exclure le poisson. Un message vertueux en totale contradiction avec l’offre des produits alimentaires et les orientations stratégiques de l’enseigne. Face à cette publicité mensongère, problématique à bien des égards, et loin d’être la première tentative d’induire les consommateurs en erreur (1), BLOOM décidait de saisir le Jury de déontologie publicitaire (2) de l’Autorité de régulation professionnelle de la publicité.

Key Points
- The Financial Times reported that Nvidia told partners including Dell and Supermicro to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. New US export controls are designed to stop Chinese companies from bypassing sales bans through foreign cloud providers.
- Dealers have listed an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs for sale as a result of the rules, CNBC reported. The supply includes thousands of B300 chips originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers.
- Cloud providers in Southeast Asia now have 90 days to apply for a license, a requirement one executive said has led to "chaos." Banks have already halted about $500 million in loans to Singapore-based provider Aolani for a planned deal with ByteDance, the Financial Times reported.
The US is closing cloud loopholes that give Chinese companies access to AI chips. Nvidia is responding by halting shipments to four countries, while thousands of high-performance processors are looking for new buyers on the secondary market.
Nvidia has told manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The Financial Times reported the halt, citing three people familiar with the matter. It isn't clear whether the pause is only temporary, according to the report.
The move follows tighter US export controls from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The rules aim to stop Chinese companies from getting around existing sales bans by renting computing power from foreign cloud providers. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC the goal was to block indirect access, including smuggling through Southeast Asia and remote access via data centers in third countries.
Thousands of B300 chips hit the market as cloud providers face chaos

Jack Duhamel, president of the AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two other insiders confirmed to CNBC that the surge is a direct result of the new rule. According to the report, sellers are looking for new buyers for hardware, including thousands of B300 chips, one of Nvidia's most advanced models. Those chips were originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers.
The rollout has created significant uncertainty in Southeast Asia, the Financial Times reported. Cloud providers have 90 days to apply for a license and prove that no restricted companies are among their end users. One cloud provider executive described the situation to the paper as chaos, saying there was no guidance on how to apply.
The fallout is also hitting major infrastructure projects. Banks have halted about $500 million in loans to Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which planned to rent computing power to TikTok parent ByteDance, the Financial Times reported. ByteDance could now pull out of the deal.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has instructed its manufacturing partners to suspend shipments of servers containing its advanced artificial intelligence processors to four Southeast Asian countries following the introduction of tighter US export restrictions, the Financial Times reported on Thursday.
Citing three people familiar with the matter, the newspaper said manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, had informed customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia would not permit their orders to be shipped.
US Tightens Restrictions on Chinese Access to Advanced AI Chips
The reported shipment suspension comes as Washington intensifies efforts to prevent Chinese technology companies from accessing Nvidia's most advanced AI processors, which are subject to restrictions on direct sales to Chinese developers.
Southeast Asia has become an important market for cloud computing infrastructure, with Chinese AI developers securing substantial computing capacity through contracts with regional data centre operators.
The US Commerce Department introduced new regulations last week aimed at restricting indirect access to advanced American semiconductor technology through overseas cloud computing services.
Cloud service providers in Asia now face a 90-day deadline to demonstrate that their services do not provide restricted entities with access to controlled technology.
Nvidia Faces Increased Scrutiny Over Regional Distribution
The issue has attracted greater attention following the recent leadership disruption at Nvidia involving Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang.
Media reports concerning Huang's personal relationships included allegations involving an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing provider accused of leasing advanced processors to Chinese developers.
The reported suspension of server shipments highlights the compliance challenges facing semiconductor manufacturers and their distribution partners as US authorities expand restrictions on access to advanced AI computing infrastructure.

L'administration Trump a donné son feu vert au gigantesque projet de centres de données dans l'espace de SpaceX. Baptisée Starmind, cette constellation pourrait compter jusqu'à un million de satellites, au grand dam des astronomes, qui redoutent une dégradation sans précédent du ciel nocturne.

SOURCE 2 (Le Grand Continent) :
Hier, mercredi 25 novembre, SpaceX a reçu de la Commission fédérale des communications (FCC) l’autorisation de déployer jusqu’à un million de satellites dans l’espace afin d’y construire des centres de données, alimentés par l’énergie solaire, destinés à l’intelligence artificielle. La décision impose à l’entreprise de mettre en service un premier satellite d’ici 2033, 10 % de la constellation d’ici 2035, la moitié d’ici 2038 et la totalité d’ici 2040 1.
Dans un communiqué, la FCC a affirmé que cette autorisation « promet de rapprocher l’humanité d’une civilisation de type Kardashev II, capable d’exploiter toute la puissance du Soleil ».
- Selon une note du groupe financier américain Evercore, SpaceX pourrait disposer d’une capacité de calcul orbitale – soit la puissance des centres de données en orbite – de 8 GW d’ici 2029, qui serait multipliée par près de 10 d’ici 2031. 2
- L’entreprise viserait alors près de quatre fois plus de capacité de calcul en orbite (77 GW) qu’au sol (20 GW), selon Bernstein.
Pour y parvenir, Evercore estime que l’entreprise de Musk devrait mener environ 909 lancements de Starship en 2029, 2 121 en 2030 et 5 657 en 2031.
- L’entreprise a mené 165 lancements orbitaux l’an dernier, mais Musk vise 10 000 lancements par an d’ici 2030.
- Afin d’atteindre cet objectif, SpaceX a annoncé fin août un projet de méga-spatioport en Louisiane qui devrait compter 10 pas de tir.
De nombreux doutes subsistent quant à la faisabilité de l’opération.
- Amazon, une entreprise concurrente de SpaceX dans le domaine spatial, a déclaré en mars, dans sa demande de rejet adressée à la FCC, qu’il faudrait « des siècles » à SpaceX pour construire cette constellation. L’entreprise a ajouté que très peu de détails avaient été donnés par SpaceX quant à la manière dont elle comptait « tenir ces promesses grandiloquentes » 3.
- L’astrophysicien américain Adam Becker a quant à lui affirmé mercredi 25 que la perspective de lancer un million de satellites dans l’espace pour créer des centres de données était une « chimère », ajoutant : « Cela n’arrivera pas » 4.
- Becker mentionne notamment une pollution accrue du ciel nocturne, ainsi qu’un risque sérieux de réaction en chaîne de collisions entre débris spatiaux, « ce qui serait une catastrophe pour l’humanité tout entière ».
Le déploiement de centres de données en orbite vise à répondre à deux problèmes auxquels fait face le secteur de l’intelligence artificielle : les besoins massifs en électricité pour alimenter les centres de données, et l’opposition de la population à leur construction. Ses promoteurs mettent également en avant le froid de l’espace pour le refroidissement des composants.
- Les financiers restent toutefois prudents face aux projets de SpaceX. Lors d’un récent emprunt de 43 milliards de dollars garanti par des puces Nvidia, les prêteurs ont tenté d’imposer une clause interdisant à l’entreprise d’envoyer ces puces en orbite, ce qui les empêcherait de les saisir et de les revendre en cas de défaut de paiement 5.
- On ignore si cette clause figure dans la version finale du contrat.

L’ESSENTIEL
- En 2026, OpenAI et Anthropic ont annoncé que leurs solutions d'IA ont trouvé des solutions à des problèmes qui résistaient obstinément aux mathématiciens.
- Pour ce faire, des essaims d’agents logiciels autonomes enchaînent raisonnement et code, puis vérifient leurs démonstrations.
- Plusieurs médaillés Fields s’inquiètent de cette production automatisée, redoutant qu’elle ne fragilise la construction théorique et la relève scientifique.
Pour beaucoup, l’année 2026 restera celle où les mathématiques ont traversé une crise identitaire, et changé à jamais. Les modèles d’IA dits « frontières » (les plus avancés), développés par OpenAI et Anthropic, ont accompli des avancées spectaculaires sur des centaines de problèmes ouverts qui déconcertaient les mathématiciens depuis des décennies, voire des siècles pour certains.
Depuis avril, des résultats tous plus impressionnants les uns que les autres ont été annoncés. Leur point commun: d'avoir été démontrés par et grace à des systèmes d'IA.
Tout a commencé par une percée d’OpenAI sur la conjecture d’Erdős sur les distances-unités et sur la conjecture jacobienne, toutes deux restées irrésolues pendant des décennies.
Puis, en septembre et en octobre, deux annonces retentissantes se sont succédé. D’abord, OpenAI a annoncé une solution au problème de Navier-Stokes, l’un des sept « problèmes du millénaire » mis en avant par l’Institut de mathématiques Clay en 2000. Ensuite, OpenAI a publié un corpus de plus de 700 articles revendiquant des solutions, des démonstrations ou des contre-exemples (qui montrent qu’une affirmation ou une conjecture est fausse) pour 372 problèmes ouverts situés à la pointe de la recherche en mathématiques.
Aujourd’hui, le chercheur d’Anthropic Levent Alpöge a annoncé une démonstration assistée par Claude (le modèle d’IA d'Anthopic) de l’hypothèse de Riemann. Il s’agit sans doute du problème le plus célèbre des mathématiques, formulé par le mathématicien allemand Bernhard Riemann en 1867.
Ce que l’on appelle désormais le « déversement d’OpenAI » (OpenAi dump) d’octobre a provoqué une onde de choc dans la communauté mathématique par son ampleur même. Hugo Duminil-Copin, professeur à l’Institut des hautes études scientifiques (IHES), à Paris, et lauréat de la médaille Fields (une distinction majeure en mathématiques), a déclaré que ce déversement avait « anéanti son domaine de recherche ». Il a également averti qu’il pourrait « démanteler » la discipline mathématique.
Si les entreprises technologiques sont parvenues à des progrès aussi stupéfiants sur des problèmes difficiles, c’est d’abord parce que leur technologie d’IA spécifique, appelée grands modèles de langage (LLM), est entraînée sur l’ensemble du corpus humain de la littérature mathématique (entre autres).
Ensuite, ces entreprises ont créé des « agents IA », des systèmes logiciels construits autour du LLM qui étendent ses capacités au raisonnement, à l’action et à l’exécution de code. Les agents peuvent aussi observer les résultats de leurs actions et agir de nouveau si nécessaire.
Pour résoudre l’équation de Navier-Stokes, OpenAI a fait collaborer 10 000 agents IA. Il a fallu 88 heures à ces agents pour trouver leur solution. 17 heures supplémentaires ont ensuite été nécessaires pour la faire vérifier grâce à un logiciel de formalisation et de vérification appelé Lean.
Read more: L’empreinte carbone astronomique des preuves mathématiques d’OpenAI
La démonstration de l’hypothèse de Riemann , réalisée par Alpöge assisté par Claude, dépasse 250 000 pages. La vérification en code Lean compte plus de 17 millions de lignes. Sa preuve en Lean a depuis été vérifiée par des chercheurs indépendants.
Contrairement à la conjecture de Poincaré, un problème du millénaire résolu par le mathématicien russe Grigori Perelman au début des années 2000, l’équation de Navier-Stokes (comme l’ensemble des 300 autres problèmes du déversement d’OpenAI) a été résolue par des agents IA presque sans intervention humaine.
C’est véritablement extraordinaire. Une métaphore pour illustrer le fonctionnement de ces agents pourrait être une colonie de termites cathédrales australiens. Chaque insecte de la colonie accomplit machinalement sa tâche locale, mais, de concert, les termites bâtissent d’impressionnants châteaux, souvent hauts de plus de six mètres, dotés d’une ventilation, d’une forme de climatisation et d’une protection contre les intempéries.
De même, chaque agent IA s’attaque à sa tâche locale, mais, collectivement, ces essaims d’agents peuvent désormais résoudre, et vérifier, les problèmes mathématiques les plus ardus qui soient.
Production en masse de résultats
Tout cela inquiète les mathématiciens. Terence Tao, professeur de mathématiques à l’Université de Californie à Los Angeles (UCLA) et lauréat de la médaille Fields en 2006, a récemment suggéré que la vitesse à laquelle l’IA produit des résultats mathématiques nuit en réalité à la discipline.
Tao a comparé ce que font les entreprises d’IA au fait de « jeter des carcasses de viande crue sur notre table en disant ‘tenez, j’ai réglé votre problème de nourriture’ ».
Le 11 septembre 2026, Tao et 25 autres médaillés Fields ont publié une déclaration affirmant que « les objectifs des entreprises d’IA et ceux de la communauté mathématique sont profondément en décalage ». La déclaration avertit que « la production en masse, à un rythme toujours plus rapide, d’énoncés ‘vrai/faux’ pourrait détruire un terreau fertile au lieu d’insuffler de nouvelles idées ».
Au moment où ces lignes sont écrites, cette déclaration compte plus de 8 000 signatures de mathématiciens dans le monde entier. Dans un esprit similaire, l’Association for Human Mathematics (« Association pour des mathématiques humaines »), récemment créée et dont les membres « s’engagent à mener une recherche entièrement sans IA, en plaçant la pensée et le jugement humains au cœur des sciences mathématiques », rassemble plus de 1 000 membres.
Il existe un vieil adage en IA connu sous le nom de paradoxe de Moravec, souvent formulé ainsi : « les problèmes difficiles sont faciles et les problèmes faciles sont difficiles ». Cette formule explique pourquoi nous disposons de machines plus performantes que nous dans des tâches que les humains jugent ardues, comme les échecs, la programmation et désormais la recherche mathématique, mais moins douées pour des gestes qui nous semblent simples, comme ranger le lave-vaisselle sans casser d’assiettes.
Les mathématiques, en un sens, ressemblent aux échecs et à la programmation. Elles forment un univers d’information relativement clos, propice à l’intervention de l’IA pour extraire des régularités, établir des liens et effectuer des calculs lui permettant de générer des résultats hors de portée humaine.
Ainsi, alors que la maîtrise et l’aisance dans les domaines mathématiques « difficiles » servaient traditionnellement d’étalon d’intelligence, tant pour les humains que pour les machines, ces puissants systèmes d’IA multi-agents montrent que la puissance de calcul brute, combinée à une abondance de données, suffit à obtenir des résultats inaccessibles à de nombreux mathématiciens sur plusieurs vies.
Un écosystème sain
Un élément annexe intéressant mérite toutefois d’être relevé : OpenAI a estimé le coût total de la recherche de la solution à l’équation de Navier-Stokes à 15 millions de dollars (environ 13,7 millions d’euros), ce qui représenterait une perte nette de 14 millions de dollars (environ 12,8 millions d’euros) si l’Institut Clay devait attribuer le prix à OpenAI.
Il est donc possible que les géants de la tech se détournent des mathématiques s’ils ne voient pas d’intérêt financier à continuer de démontrer des conjectures ouvertes.
En abordant un problème de manière « ascendante » (bottom-up), les mathématiciens bâtissent des théories et tissent des liens entre des sous-disciplines en apparence éloignées. Ils diffusent leurs découvertes préliminaires et leurs résultats partiels dans des revues, des conférences et des ateliers.
Ce dialogue avec le reste de la communauté inclut les doctorants et les jeunes chercheurs, ce qui permet de former une nouvelle génération de mathématiciens appelés à faire avancer le domaine.
Nombre d’étudiants en mathématiques s’orientent ensuite vers des secteurs où une solide formation mathématique est précieuse, comme l’administration publique, la science des données, l’éducation, le développement durable, la finance et la cybersécurité. Cet écosystème, essentiel à la vitalité d’une société et d’une économie, pourrait être menacé si une nouvelle approche « descendante » (top-down), en boîte noire et fondée sur la rétro-ingénierie, devenait une nouvelle norme.
Ainsi, si le fait de disposer d’outils d’IA puissants pour résoudre des problèmes anciens ouvre des perspectives nouvelles et stimulantes (je suis même convaincu qu’il n’y a jamais eu de meilleur moment pour étudier les mathématiques), ces possibilités doivent être soigneusement mises en balance avec les intérêts plus larges de la discipline comme avec ceux de la société.

depeches.resume: L’Olympique Lyonnais a été accroché par les Norvégiens de Lilleström (0-0) jeudi soir lors de la 5e journée de Ligue Europa. Un match qui s’est terminé par deux décisions arbitrales qui auraient pu être favorables aux Gones sans l’intervention de l’arbitrage vidéo.

depeches.titre: OL-Lillestrom SK: tenu en échec, Lyon voit la qualification directe s'éloigner
depeches.resume: L'OL avait un bon coup à jouer pour la qualification directe en recevant une formation norvégienne a priori bien plus faible, pour cette 5e journée de Ligue Europa. depeches.resume: Des incidents ont opposé les forces de l’ordre à des supporters de Besiktas, opposé aux Israéliens de Hapoel Beer-Sheva (2-1) jeudi soir dans ce match de Ligue Europa délocalisé à Batoumi, en Géorgie. depeches.resume: Une rixe a éclaté dans les tribunes du Vélodrome avant le match OM-Levski Sofia, jeudi soir lors de la 5e journée de Ligue Europa (1-0). Après le match, les autorités ont communiqué un lourd bilan.

depeches.titre: Messi et Ronaldo bientôt réunis dans la même équipe: le rêve de Tevez pour son jubilé en bonne voie
depeches.resume: L’ancien buteur de l’Argentine, Carlos Tevez, a confirmé la venue de Lionel Messi pour son jubilé le 20 décembre à la Bombonera. Il attend désormais la réponse de Cristiano Ronaldo. CR7 et la Pulga pourraient jouer pour la première fois dans la même équipe.

depeches.titre: OM-Levski Sofia: Genesio n'a pas aimé la panenka ratée par Gouiri
depeches.resume: Si Marseille a décroché un succès important ce jeudi face au Levski Sofia (1-0) en Ligue Europa, Bruno Genesio n'a pas franchement apprécié la panenka tentée par Amine Gouiri en seconde période.

depeches.titre: La Coupe de France sur France TV: il faut encore patienter
depeches.resume: La pression est de taille pour la diffusion TV de la Coupe de France. La FFF doit encore patienter.

depeches.titre: Mercato: Lucas Chevalier envisage un départ du PSG
depeches.resume: Comme annoncé jeudi par L’Equipe, le gardien du PSG, Lucas Chevalier, n°2 derrière Matveï Safonov, n’exclut pas un départ cet hiver pour retrouver du temps de jeu.

depeches.titre: Euro espoirs: la France hérite en poule de l'Angleterre, double tenante du titre
depeches.resume: Qualifiés pour l'Euro 2027, les Bleuets viseront la victoire finale ainsi que la qualification pour les JO 2028 de Los Angeles.

depeches.titre: OM-Levski Sofia: la vidéo de l'incroyable panenka ratée de Gouiri sur penalty

depeches.resume: Délocalisé en Géorgie, le match de la cinquième journée de Ligue Europa entre Besiktas (Turquie) et l'Hapoël Beer Sheva (Israël) a été interrompu. Selon plusieurs médias turcs, la police géorgienne est intervenue de manière musclée dans les tribunes après qu'un drapeau palestinien a été brandi.

depeches.titre: Assou-Ekotto explique pourquoi il s'est battu avec Moukandjo pendant Cameroun-Croatie au Mondial 2024
depeches.resume: L’ancien arrière gauche du Cameroun, Benoît Assou-Ekotto (24 sélections), a raconté dans l’émission Lockin son embrouille avec son équipier Benjamin Moukandjo lors du match du Mondial 2014 face à la Croatie.

depeches.resume: L’ancien milieu de terrain international Sabri Lamouchi est l’invité de Riolo Club. depeches.titre: "Avec ton talent, je me bats pour le Ballon d'or chaque année", le sentiment d'inachevé de Sabri Lamouchi pour Hatem Ben Arfa
depeches.resume: Invité du Riolo Club, Sabri Lamouchi, ancien international français, est revenu sur son passage à Rennes où il a connu Hatem Ben Arfa pendant quelques mois en 2018. Il conserve le souvenir d'un des joueurs les plus talentueux croisés même si sa carrière n'a pas trop été en adéquation avec ce talent.

depeches.resume: Nommé en janvier 2026 au poste de sélectionneur de la Tunisie, Sabri Lamouchi a été démis de ses fonctions cinq mois plus tard, après la lourde défaite des Aigles de Carthage pour leur entrée en lice en Coupe du monde (5-1 contre la Suède).
